beats.script_body: As the ferry crosses the harbor, step out onto the deck and look to your left for Governors Island — the 176-acre former U.S. Army and then Coast Guard base, closed in 1996. Almost half of it, eighty-five acres, is a National Historic Landmark, and five individual structures are landmarked as well. The three-story fort protecting the island on this side is Castle Williams, built between 1807 and 1811, one of three forts on the island.

beats.source_passage: Immediately to your left will be Governors Island. This is the 176-acre former U.S. Army and then Coast Guard base that was closed in 1996. Almost half (eighty-five acres) of the island is a National Historic Landmark, and there are five individual landmarked structures as well. At this time the future of the island is unclear, but everything from casinos to universities has been proposed. beats.script_body: Ferries have crossed this harbor since sailing vessels began running between the islands as early as 1713. The first steamer-ferry service between Staten Island and Manhattan was started by Daniel Tompkins, who launched the Nautilus in 1817; regular service has continued ever since. In 1905 municipal ferries began replacing the private companies, and the city has run the route ever since.

beats.script_body: Built by architects Carrere & Hastings between 1904 and 1906, Staten Island Borough Hall is the main government building for the borough. It was designed to be immediately noticed by those arriving by ferry from Manhattan, standing as a symbol of Staten Island's equal membership in greater New York, and it is a New York City Landmark. Carrere & Hastings was one of the city's more prominent early-twentieth-century firms — and one wonders whether the fact that John Carrere was a Staten Island resident helped land this plum contract.

beats.trigger_address: 105 Hamilton Avenue at St. Marks Place
beats.script_body: Built in 1904 in the collegiate Gothic style, Curtis High School was the first public high school on Staten Island and the first municipal building put up after the 1898 Consolidation of Greater New York. It is named for George William Curtis, a nineteenth-century writer and editor who kept a country estate on the island — an early advocate of women's suffrage and of professional civil service as a cure for political corruption. Locally he is remembered for sheltering Horace Greeley from pro-Confederate Staten Islanders during the Civil War. Curtis wrote for Harper's and The Nation and published Putnam's Monthly with his friend and fellow Staten Islander Frederick Law Olmsted.

beats.script_body: Behind the iron fence and Greek Revival buildings stands Sailors' Snug Harbor, created in 1801 with a bequest from shipping merchant Robert R. Randall as an institution for the care of "aged, decrepit, and worn-out sailors." Snug Harbor bought this land in 1831 and built a campus for retired seamen; by 1900 it housed over a thousand people. As the number of American sailors dwindled, so did the institution — in 1975 it relocated to North Carolina, and a year later the complex became the Sailors' Snug Harbor Cultural Center.

beats.script_body: There have been fortifications on this site since 1663, and it was one of the last British positions to surrender after the American Revolution. The present fort was built in 1847 and dedicated in 1865 to Brigadier General James Wadsworth, following his death at the Civil War's Battle of the Wilderness. Since the early 1990s the installation has been part of the Gateway National Recreation Area, with a National Park Service visitor center, a short film on the history of New York's fortifications, and a scenic overlook on Tompkins Road.

beats.script_body: When the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge was completed in 1964, designed by Swiss engineer Othmar Ammann, it was the world's longest suspension bridge, measuring 4,260 feet between its towers. It is no longer the longest, but it is still beautiful. Many Italian Americans in Bay Ridge, near the Brooklyn approach, did not want their homes destroyed for its approaches — and naming the bridge after Giovanni da Verrazano, who sailed into New York Harbor in 1524, was hardly enough to soothe their concerns. It took Robert Moses many years to beat back the opposition, but he eventually got his way: eight thousand Brooklynites lost their homes, and a good number more moved across the bridge to Staten Island. The Staten Island side is the starting point for the New York Marathon every November. Including its approaches the bridge runs 13,700 feet; it stands 228 feet above the water; each tower is 693 feet tall; and it costs seven dollars to cross — though the toll is collected only traveling from Brooklyn to Staten Island, so going this way you get a free ride.

beats.script_body: Coney Island takes its name from an Anglicized version of the Dutch word for rabbit — the animals were abundant here in the 1600s. A vacation spot for New Yorkers since at least the mid-nineteenth century, it eventually held three of the most spectacular amusement parks in the nation: Steeplechase Park, Luna Park, and Dreamland. All are closed now; in their place stands Astroland, opened in 1954. From the boardwalk, look right to a large pier where residents fish and go crabbing, and where the Polar Bear Club swims every weekend through the winter — its New Year's Day plunge drawing news cameras and one-time swimmers from across the city.

beats.script_body: The intersection of Gravesend Neck Road and McDonald Avenue was the town center of Gravesend, the only non-Dutch town among the original six settlements that made up seventeenth-century Brooklyn. Gravesend was founded in 1643 by Lady Deborah Moody, an Anabaptist who fled religious intolerance in Massachusetts — and here became the first woman to vote at a town meeting. The name comes either from the Dutch grafesande, read as both "end of the grove" and "count's beach," or from the British town of Gravesend.

beats.script_body: Ocean Parkway, finished in 1876 before the automobile, stretches six miles from Coney Island to Prospect Park. Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, who designed both Central Park in Manhattan and Prospect Park in Brooklyn, believed strongly in a network of scenic parkways throughout the city, and this is one of them. It originally had a central drive, greenery-filled malls — hence "parkway" — a bridle trail, and pedestrian walkways. The bridle trails are now service roads, but the beauty of the parkway remains.

beats.script_body: Just off one of Brooklyn's busiest commercial streets, the small historic district of Prospect Park South hides large single-family houses ranging from Tudor to Queen Anne to neo-Japanese. The neighborhood was created by developer Dean Alvord, who bought forty acres here in 1899. To shape the place he wanted, Alvord required houses set back thirty-nine feet from the sidewalk, with eight feet between street and sidewalk left for greenery. Most of the houses were finished by 1905.

beats.script_body: The 526-acre Prospect Park was designed by Calvert Vaux and Frederick Law Olmsted in 1866–1873, as soon as they finished Central Park. Like Central Park it gathers different landscapes — the long, hilly Long Meadow, a wooded ravine, a lake, several arches, and a number of buildings. And as in Manhattan, the city first backed a mediocre design by Egbert Viele before abandoning it for Vaux and Olmsted's. Many find Prospect Park as beautiful as Central Park, if not more so, thanks to the very high hills that crop up in several places.

beats.script_body: Built in 1694, the Friends Meeting House on Northern Boulevard is the oldest house of worship in New York City. It keeps the traditional Quaker spirit — without decoration or art, to allow undistracted worship — and during the Revolutionary War the British converted it into a prison and hospital. Step inside if you can: the second story rests on massive forty-foot hand-cut oak beams, and the original handmade ironwork is still in use. The Meeting House is on the National Register of Historic Places, and visitors are welcome.

beats.script_body: Built in the colonial saltbox style in 1661 by John Bowne — an Englishman who reached Flushing by way of Boston — the Bowne House became a flashpoint for religious freedom. After converting to the Quaker faith, Bowne invited Quakers to meet in his kitchen, defying New Amsterdam governor Peter Stuyvesant, who had declared the Dutch Reformed Church the only acceptable order. When Stuyvesant moved against the Quakers, thirty townspeople signed the "Flushing Remonstrance," protesting that they could not "stretch our hands against them, to punish, banish or persecute them." Stuyvesant responded by arresting and fining the signers, and in 1662 he arrested Bowne himself, sentencing him to prison and banishment. After seven months in jail, Bowne sailed to the Netherlands and argued before the Dutch West India Company for religious tolerance; they freed him and rebuked Stuyvesant with a letter upholding the principle. Many historians regard this community resistance as a foundation of the First Amendment's freedom of religion. Nine generations of Bownes lived here, the last leaving in 1945; the house is now called "A National Shrine to Religious Freedom."

beats.script_body: The modern red-brick house at 34-56 107th Street is the Louis Armstrong House, a National Historic Landmark and the home of jazz great Louis Armstrong for twenty-nine years, from 1942 until his death in 1971. Born in the Storyville neighborhood of New Orleans, Armstrong grew up amid the ragtime and blues that shaped his life; his musical career began in the marching band of the Colored Waifs' Home, where he was sent in 1912. His professional career got a boost when King Oliver made him second cornetist in 1922, bringing him to Chicago, and he reached New York as a trumpeter, joining Fats Waller and Edith Wilson's Broadway revue Hot Chocolate in 1929. He performed in numerous shows and films, returning to the stage in 1947; among his greatest hits are "Blueberry Hill" of 1949, "Mack the Knife" of 1955, and "Hello Dolly" of 1962.

beats.script_body: Past the train tracks lies Forest Hills Gardens, a 142-acre community planned by Frederick Law Olmsted Jr. — son of the Central Park Olmsted — in the style of an English Tudor village. Construction began around 1910, but two world wars and the 1929 crash meant most houses weren't built until the 1940s and 1950s. Olmsted, with his colleague Grosvenor Atterbury, designed the railroad station, the greens, and nearby houses. The community was originally envisioned by Margaret Olivia Slocum Sage, wife of financier-philanthropist Russell Sage and founder of the Russell Sage Foundation.

beats.script_body: Farmland in the early twentieth century, the Jackson Heights Historic District was ripe for speculative building just before the Queensboro Bridge opened in 1909. The Queensboro Realty Company bought up 350 acres and built the neighborhood over two decades. Its innovation lay in the blocks themselves — five- and six-story cooperative apartment houses with large rear gardens along the avenues, smaller attached single-family houses on the side streets. But in the 1920s the company tolerated "red-lining," an exclusionary policy directed against Jews, Catholics, and African Americans that blocked them from mortgages. Today Jackson Heights is a thriving, ethnically diverse community, home in the early 1990s to the largest Argentinean community in the city.

beats.script_body: The Bronx is New York's northernmost borough and the only one wholly on the mainland of the United States. It is named for Jonas Bronck, an early settler. Parts of the western Bronx were annexed by New York in 1875, and the eastern parts joined the city at the 1898 Consolidation. The borough became a destination for millions leaving Manhattan's tenements in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, who then moved on to the suburbs in the 1960s and 1970s. Over twenty percent of the Bronx is parkland.

beats.script_body: The Grand Concourse stretches four and a half miles from the South Bronx northward and is 180 feet wide at its broadest. Completed south to 161st Street between 1902 and 1909 and extended later in the 1930s, the concourse became home to some of the Bronx's most elegant apartment buildings, especially in the 1920s and 1930s. At first only the service roads carried cars, with the larger center stretch reserved for horses and carriages; now everything is a car lane.

beats.script_body: Bronx Community College began in 1894 as the uptown campus of Greenwich Village's New York University; in 1973 NYU sold the grounds to the city, which turned them into BCC. The Hall of Fame Terrace, open to the public, was designed by McKim, Mead and White — a semicircular arcade with bronze busts of educators, lawyers, scientists, and others, giving a great westward view. Cleverly, the Hall of Fame was designed to hide the giant foundation walls of buildings Stanford White designed for the campus.

beats.script_body: On the corner stands Poe Cottage, built in 1816. The American author Edgar Allan Poe moved here in 1846, hoping the then-country air would cure his wife's tuberculosis. She died soon after they moved, but Poe stayed on until just before his own death in 1849, writing "Ulalume" and "The Bells" here. The cottage originally stood across the street and was moved to its current location in 1913.

beats.script_body: Wave Hill is a nonprofit, city-owned park in Riverdale, its beautiful grounds holding an excellent herb garden and a small greenhouse. Wave Hill House, on the grounds, was a country home built in 1843, and over the years it has sheltered Teddy Roosevelt in the summers of 1870 and 1871, Mark Twain from 1901 to 1903, and Arturo Toscanini from 1942 to 1945. Bashford Dean, zoologist and curator of arms and armor for the Metropolitan Museum, lived in Glyndor House, another building on the grounds.

beats.poi_name: Ellis Island National Museum of Immigration
beats.script_body: Further into the harbor, to your right, are Ellis Island and the Statue of Liberty. Ellis Island first opened as New York's immigration reception center in 1892, and its main building — now a museum — opened in 1900. Between its opening and 1924, some sixteen million immigrants entered America through this building. The island itself began as a 3.3-acre sandbar; to meet the demand for space, landfill grew it to its current 27.5 acres.
